title: Society as a Graph
description: From Simmel's dyads to sociometry — why social life is structurally relational

concepts.title: Simmel and the Form of Social Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Georg Simmel, writing around 1900, argued that sociology should study not the contents of interaction but its forms — the geometric patterns of association that recur across cultures and centuries.

His most famous distinction is between the dyad (two people) and the triad (three). A dyad is fragile: if one person leaves, the relationship vanishes. A triad is qualitatively different — it can sustain coalitions, mediation, and the tertius gaudens ('the rejoicing third') who profits from the conflict of the other two.

Adding a single third person transforms the moral and strategic landscape. Simmel saw this as evidence that structure has its own causal power: the same individuals behave differently in differently shaped groups. Network science begins from this Simmelian insight — society is not just an aggregate of individuals but a pattern of ties, and the pattern itself does work.

concepts.title: Moreno's Sociometry
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacob Moreno's Who Shall Survive? (1934) introduced the sociogram — a hand-drawn diagram representing people as points and their relationships as lines. Studying a New York girls' reformatory, Moreno mapped friendship choices and showed that runaway clusters could be predicted from the network structure.

Sociometry was the first systematic attempt to measure social structure. Moreno asked subjects whom they would choose for tasks, lunch, or roommates, then tallied stars (highly chosen individuals), isolates (chosen by no one), and cliques (mutually connected groups).

This was sociology's break from pure narrative description. Moreno demonstrated that intervention required structural knowledge: rearranging which dorms held which residents, based on the sociogram, reduced conflict. Network analysis still uses his core move — translating relational data into a graph and reading the graph as a map of social forces.

concepts.title: Nodes, Edges, and Density
concepts.contentHtml:
A social network is a graph: a set of nodes (also called vertices or actors) connected by edges (ties, links, relations). Edges may be directed (advice flows from A to B) or undirected (A and B are friends), and may carry weights for strength or frequency.

Three properties matter immediately:

Reciprocity: the proportion of directed ties that are mutual. High reciprocity in advice networks suggests trust; low reciprocity suggests hierarchy.
Transitivity: if A is tied to B and B to C, is A tied to C? Social networks are far more transitive than random graphs — friends of friends really do tend to be friends.
Density: the fraction of possible ties that are actually present. Most social networks are remarkably sparse — densities of 1–5% — yet still keep nearly everyone reachable through short chains. This combination of sparseness and reachability is what makes structural analysis interesting.

title: The Strength of Weak Ties
description: Granovetter's argument that distant acquaintances move information

concepts.title: Granovetter's Insight
concepts.contentHtml:
Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper The Strength of Weak Ties is one of the most cited articles in social science. Its claim is counter-intuitive: the relationships that matter most for moving information through a society are not your closest friends but your weak ties — acquaintances, former colleagues, friends-of-friends.

Granovetter defined tie strength informally as a combination of time spent, emotional intensity, intimacy, and reciprocal services. He then made a structural argument. Strong ties tend to cluster: your close friends are usually friends with each other. So information circulating among them quickly becomes redundant — they all know what you know.

Weak ties, by contrast, often connect you to people in different social circles. They are the channels through which novel information enters your life. The paradox is sharp: distant relationships, precisely because they are distant, carry more news than intimate ones.

concepts.title: Bridges and the Forbidden Triad
concepts.contentHtml:
Granovetter formalised his intuition with a structural claim. Suppose A has a strong tie to B and a strong tie to C. He argued that B and C are then very likely to be at least weakly tied themselves — strong ties produce closure. The forbidden triad (A strongly tied to both B and C, but B and C with no tie at all) is empirically rare.

It follows that bridges — ties that are the only path between two parts of the network — must be weak. A strong tie cannot be a bridge, because closure would have produced a shortcut around it.

This is the structural core of the argument. If you want information to cross a community boundary, it must travel along a weak tie. The result reframes social capital: bridging weak ties are not relational filler but load-bearing infrastructure for the diffusion of jobs, gossip, and innovation.

concepts.title: Getting a Job
concepts.contentHtml:
In Getting a Job (1974), Granovetter tested the theory empirically. He surveyed professional and managerial workers in the Boston suburb of Newton who had recently changed jobs, asking how they found their new position.

Among those who heard about their job through a personal contact, only about 17% described that contact as someone they saw 'often'. Roughly 28% saw the contact 'occasionally', and the majority — over 55% — had seen the contact 'rarely', often only once or twice a year.

The contacts who delivered the most useful job leads were therefore weak ties. Strong ties shared the same information pool already known to the job-seeker; weak ties bridged into pools the seeker could not otherwise reach.

The finding has been replicated across labour markets and recently re-examined at LinkedIn scale by Rajkumar and colleagues (2022), who found that moderately weak ties produced the most job mobility — a striking modern confirmation of a fifty-year-old theory.

title: Structural Holes and Centrality
description: Burt's brokers and Freeman's measures of network position

concepts.title: Burt's Structural Holes
concepts.contentHtml:
Ronald Burt's Structural Holes (1992) sharpened Granovetter's argument. A structural hole is a gap between two clusters that lack a direct connection. The actor whose ties span the hole becomes a broker, controlling the flow of information and opportunity between otherwise disconnected groups.

Burt revived Simmel's tertius gaudens: the third who benefits from the disconnection of the other two. Brokers enjoy three advantages — access to non-redundant information, timing (they hear about opportunities first), and arbitrage (they can play one side against the other or translate between them).

Burt's empirical work in firms — most notably at Raytheon — showed that managers whose networks were rich in structural holes received better performance reviews, generated more good ideas, and were promoted faster. The structural position was a stronger predictor than human capital. Where you are in the network shapes what you can do.

concepts.title: Degree, Closeness, and Betweenness
concepts.contentHtml:
Linton Freeman's 1979 synthesis defined three foundational centrality measures, each capturing a different idea of what it means to be central.

Degree centrality is simply the number of ties a node has. A high-degree node is locally popular and well-connected.

Closeness centrality measures how short the average path is from a node to everyone else. A high-closeness node hears news quickly and can reach others efficiently.

Betweenness centrality counts how often a node lies on the shortest path between other pairs. High-betweenness nodes are gatekeepers and brokers — they control flow even when they are not themselves popular.

The three need not coincide. A celebrity may have huge degree but low betweenness if their followers are themselves well-connected. A receptionist may have modest degree but enormous betweenness if every internal communication routes through her. Asking which centrality matters forces you to specify what is flowing.

concepts.title: Eigenvector Centrality and PageRank
concepts.contentHtml:
The deepest centrality measure asks not just how many ties a node has but whose ties. Eigenvector centrality assigns each node a score proportional to the sum of its neighbours' scores. The result is the principal eigenvector of the adjacency matrix: a node is important if it is connected to other important nodes.

Phillip Bonacich introduced eigenvector centrality to sociology in 1972. It captures social intuitions about prestige: an introduction from a well-connected person counts more than the same introduction from an isolate.

Eigenvector centrality became globally famous when Sergey Brin and Larry Page adapted it for the web in 1998. PageRank treats hyperlinks as endorsements and computes a damped eigenvector to rank pages. Their PhD project became Google. The bridge from Bonacich's sociology paper to the trillion-dollar search engine is direct: a centrality measure designed to capture social prestige turned out to capture web authority too. Network position is fungible across domains.

title: Small Worlds and Scale-Free Networks
description: Six degrees, clustering, and the rich-get-richer dynamics of real networks

concepts.title: Milgram's Six Degrees
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1967 Stanley Milgram ran his now-famous chain-letter experiment. Volunteers in Nebraska and Kansas were asked to forward a folder to a stockbroker in Boston, but only by passing it to someone they knew on a first-name basis. Each recipient repeated the rule.

For chains that completed, the median number of intermediaries was around five or six — the origin of the phrase 'six degrees of separation', popularised by John Guare's 1990 play.

Milgram's experiment had genuine flaws — most chains never completed, and Judith Kleinfeld later showed that the original sample was small and selected. Yet larger studies have broadly confirmed the qualitative finding. A 2011 Facebook study covering 721 million users measured an average distance of about 4.7. The world is astonishingly compact. Despite seven billion people and dense local clustering, almost everyone is reachable through a handful of hops.

concepts.title: Watts and Strogatz
concepts.contentHtml:
Why is the world a small world? Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz answered in a 1998 Nature paper that became one of the founding documents of network science.

They considered a regular ring lattice in which each node connects only to its nearest neighbours. Such a graph has high clustering (your neighbours' neighbours are mostly your neighbours) but long average path lengths. A purely random graph has the opposite: short paths but almost no clustering.

Watts and Strogatz showed that rewiring just a tiny fraction of the lattice's edges to random distant nodes collapses the average path length dramatically while leaving clustering largely intact. The result is the small-world regime: high clustering plus short paths.

Real social networks live there. A few long-range shortcuts — the friend who moved abroad, the conference acquaintance — are enough to fuse densely-clustered local communities into a globally connected whole.

concepts.title: Barabási–Albert and Power Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
The other surprising fact about real networks is that their degree distributions are extremely uneven. A few nodes have enormously many ties; most have very few. Albert-László Barabási and Réka Albert showed in 1999 that this scale-free structure follows a power-law: the probability of having degree k is proportional to roughly k to the negative gamma, with gamma typically between 2 and 3.

Their explanation was a generative model with two ingredients: growth (nodes join over time) and preferential attachment (new nodes prefer to connect to nodes that are already well-connected). Together these produce 'the rich get richer' — a Yule–Simon process rediscovered for networks.

Scale-free networks are robust to random failure but vulnerable to targeted attack on hubs. They diffuse information rapidly through hubs but exhibit large inequalities in influence. Power-law fits are sometimes overstated — Aaron Clauset and colleagues argue many networks fit log-normal distributions equally well — but the qualitative point survives: real social networks are spectacularly heterogeneous.

title: Diffusion, Homophily, and Social Capital
description: How behaviours spread, why birds of a feather flock, and what networks give us

concepts.title: Simple and Complex Contagion
concepts.contentHtml:
Ideas, behaviours, and diseases spread through networks — but not all in the same way. Simple contagion (information, viruses) can be transmitted by a single contact. Complex contagion (costly or controversial behaviours: protest, vaccination, lifestyle change) typically requires multiple independent sources of social reinforcement before adoption.

Mark Granovetter modelled this in 1978 with threshold models: each individual has a personal threshold — the fraction of contacts who must adopt before they do. A small distribution change can flip a population from quiescence to a full cascade.

Damon Centola's experiments (2010 onward) show empirically that complex contagions actually spread better through clustered networks than through small-world shortcuts — the opposite of simple contagion. Long-range weak ties carry information well but social proof poorly. The kind of structure that helps a rumour can hinder a movement.

concepts.title: Birds of a Feather
concepts.contentHtml:
Miller McPherson, Lynn Smith-Lovin, and James Cook's 2001 review article 'Birds of a Feather' established homophily — the tendency of similar people to associate — as one of the most robust regularities in social science. Across race, age, religion, education, occupation, and gender, ties are far more likely than chance among similar individuals.

They distinguished baseline homophily (induced by demographic availability — you can only befriend who is around) from inbreeding homophily (preference beyond what mere availability would predict).

Homophily has profound consequences. It segregates information, reinforces inequality, and explains why advice, opportunity, and culture move along demographic lines. McPherson and colleagues argue that homophily is the structural source of much of what looks like prejudice — the world is sorted before any individual chooses. Understanding homophily is therefore prerequisite to understanding why bridging weak ties are so rare and so consequential when they exist.

concepts.title: Social Capital: Bonding and Bridging
concepts.contentHtml:
Social capital — the resources individuals access through their network ties — has been theorised in three influential strands.

James Coleman emphasised closure: dense networks enforce norms and trust, making cooperation possible. Pierre Bourdieu treated social capital as a class resource, alongside economic and cultural capital. Nan Lin saw it as instrumental access to resources embedded in others.

Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) drew the distinction that has stuck: bonding social capital connects similar people within a group (family, ethnic enclave), while bridging social capital connects across difference. Bonding helps you 'get by'; bridging helps you 'get ahead'. Putnam argued that American civic life had eroded across the late twentieth century, with declining membership in clubs, churches, and bowling leagues — the title's image.

Critics including Claude Fischer challenge Putnam's measurements, but the bonding-bridging distinction has become standard. It maps directly onto network structure: bonding is dense closure, bridging is weak ties spanning structural holes.
